produced_findings.claim: Non-atomic check-then-set in `decrement_stock` oversells stock under concurrency (TOCTOU) The function reads `stock = get_stock(sku)` on line 13, checks `stock < qty` on line 14, and writes `set_stock(sku, stock - qty)` on line 16. It takes no lock, transaction, or compare-and-set, and `set_stock` writes an absolute value computed from the earlier read. The docstring says this runs on the checkout hot path for every confirmed order, so overlapping calls for the same SKU are expected. Two concurrent orders for the same SKU can both read the same stock, for example 5, and both pass the check. Each then writes `5 - qty`, so one decrement is lost and stock is overstated. Alternatively, two orders that together exceed stock can both succeed, which is overselling. Inventory then drifts from reality, and the drift grows with checkout traffic. `reserve_stock` has the same check-then-act shape, but this diff did not change it. This finding covers only the newly added function.

produced_findings.claim: Reservation check-then-update is not atomic and can oversell stock `reserve_item` reads `count = get_count(sku)`, checks `count < quantity`, then writes `_inventory[sku] = count - quantity` from the stale local `count`. No lock or atomic operation covers the read, check and write, and the app runs with `app.run(threaded=True)`. Two concurrent requests for `widget` (stock 5, quantity 5 each) can both read 5, both pass the check, and both write 0. Both get 200, so 10 units are sold from 5. A concurrent reservation can also be lost (lost update), leaving the stored count wrong. In-memory state is per-process, so the lock fixes the threaded case but not several workers. Each worker would hold its own `_inventory`, which is a separate problem to resolve before real deployment.

Negative or zero `quantity` is not rejected, so a reservation can add stock `quantity = int(request.json["quantity"])` is used with no bounds check. For `quantity = -100`, `count < quantity` is false, so `_inventory[sku] = count - (-100)` increases stock. For an unknown `sku`, `get_count` returns 0, and `0 < -5` is false, so a new SKU is created with positive stock. Any caller can inflate inventory or create phantom SKUs with a single request, which corrupts stock data and defeats the oversell guard.

Malformed or missing request body and out-of-stock both surface as 500 `request.json["quantity"]` raises on a missing key or a non-JSON body, `int(...)` raises `ValueError` on a non-numeric value, and `raise OutOfStock(sku)` has no `errorhandler` registered anywhere in the module. Flask turns each of these into a generic 500 or 400/415 response. A normal business outcome (insufficient stock) and bad client input are indistinguishable from server faults. This produces error-log noise and gives clients no usable status or message, but it does not corrupt state.

produced_findings.claim: Stored XSS: webhook `sender` is interpolated into admin HTML unescaped `receive_webhook` (line 7-8) stores whatever JSON it receives, and `render_admin_summary` (line 13) puts `e['sender']` straight into an f-string `{...}`. There is no `html.escape`, no template auto-escaping, and no validation of the type or content of `sender`. A body like `{"sender": ""}` is returned verbatim in the admin markup. Any party that can POST to the webhook can run script in an administrator's browser when they open the summary. That allows session theft and actions performed as the admin. The attacker controls the payload and the victim is a privileged user.

Webhook accepts unauthenticated, unvalidated input, so one bad event breaks the admin view `receive_webhook` does no signature or secret check on the sender. It does no schema check either, so any valid JSON is stored: a list, a number, or a dict without `sender`. Malformed JSON raises an uncaught `json.JSONDecodeError`. `render_admin_summary` then indexes `e['sender']` for every stored event. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can inject events, which makes F1 exploitable remotely. A single stored payload that is not a dict with a `sender` key (for example `{}` or `[]`) makes `render_admin_summary` raise `KeyError` or `TypeError` on every later call. The admin view stays down until the process restarts, because events are never removed.

Unbounded in-memory event store `_events` is a module-level list that only grows, and no size cap is applied to the body or the list. Sustained or large posts grow process memory without limit. Events are also lost on restart and are not shared across workers. This is a robustness concern and does not block.

produced_findings.claim: `decrement_stock` check-then-write is not atomic, so concurrent orders oversell stock `get_stock` (line 13), the `stock < qty` guard (line 14) and `set_stock(sku, stock - qty)` (line 16) are separate calls. Suppose two orders each read stock = 5 and each request 5. Both pass the guard, and both write 0. Ten units are sold from five. A different interleaving gives a lost update: A reads 10, B reads 10, A writes 7, B writes 8, and the stock is wrong. The result is overselling and a corrupted inventory count. The check does not protect against the very concurrency it is guarding, and the failure is silent because nothing raises. `reserve_stock` has the same read-then-act shape, but it is outside this delta, so it is not reported here. It is still worth fixing consistently when this is corrected. The difference is that `decrement_stock` also writes back a value computed from the stale read, so it can both oversell and lose updates.

produced_findings.claim: Reserve is a non-atomic read-check-write; concurrent requests oversell stock `count = get_count(sku)` reads the shared module-level `_inventory`. The check `count < quantity` runs on that stale local value, and `_inventory[sku] = count - quantity` writes back a value computed from it. No lock or atomic operation covers the sequence. The app is started with `app.run(threaded=True)`, so requests run on concurrent threads. Two requests for 5 widgets, both with `count == 5`, can both pass the check, and both then write `0`. Both get a 200 while 10 widgets were reserved against a stock of 5. Interleavings where one request's write overwrites another's (lost update) have the same effect. Inventory is oversold and the stored count no longer matches the units reserved. Under load the stock figure can't be trusted.

Negative or zero `quantity` is accepted and inflates stock `quantity = int(request.json["quantity"])` is not range-checked. For `quantity = -3` the guard `count < quantity` is never true, and `_inventory[sku] = count - (-3)` increases the count. The `reserve` route has no authorization or sign check. Any caller can create stock by posting a negative quantity, which corrupts inventory. A quantity of 0 is a meaningless no-op reservation that returns 200.

`OutOfStock` is raised but never handled, so an expected business outcome becomes HTTP 500 `raise OutOfStock(sku)` has no `@app.errorhandler(OutOfStock)` and no try/except in the view. Flask turns the uncaught exception into a generic 500 and logs a stack trace. Nothing else in the diff references `OutOfStock`. Clients can't tell "insufficient stock" from a server fault, so they may retry or alert on it. Normal sold-out traffic floods the error logs with traces.

Malformed bodies and unknown SKUs are not handled `request.json["quantity"]` raises a 400/415 or `KeyError` (500) when the body is missing, not JSON, or lacks `quantity`. `int(...)` raises `ValueError` (500) on non-numeric input. For an unknown `sku`, `get_count` returns 0 and the request is reported as out of stock rather than not found. On a 0-quantity request, an unknown SKU would be inserted into `_inventory` with a count of 0. Client input errors surface as 500s. Unknown SKUs can be added to the inventory map as a side effect.

produced_findings.claim: Stored XSS: webhook `sender` is rendered into admin HTML unescaped `receive_webhook` stores the parsed payload as-is (line 8). `render_admin_summary` then puts `e['sender']` into an f-string `<td>` with no HTML escaping (line 13). Nothing in the file validates or sanitizes `sender`. A webhook with `{"sender": "<script>…</script>"}` runs in the browser of any admin who views the summary. The attacker can steal the session, perform admin actions, or pivot. The write path has no authentication (see F2), so any internet caller can plant the payload.

Webhook endpoint accepts events without authenticating the caller `receive_webhook` parses and stores whatever body it is given. It does no signature or HMAC check, shared-secret check, or timestamp check, and it takes no headers. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can forge events, which also reaches the F1 injection and the F4 growth. Receivers of third-party webhooks are normally expected to verify a signature over the raw body.

One malformed event permanently breaks the admin summary `json.loads` output is stored without checking its type or shape. It is not guaranteed to be a dict with a `sender` key. Invalid JSON raises `JSONDecodeError` out of `receive_webhook` with no handling. `render_admin_summary` indexes `e['sender']` for every stored event (line 13). A body such as `{}`, `[]`, or `{"x":1}` is stored and returns `ok`. Every later call to `render_admin_summary` then raises `KeyError` or `TypeError`, and the summary stays broken until the process restarts. Any single sender can disable the admin view for everyone.

Unbounded, unsynchronized in-memory event store `_events` is a module-level list that grows on every request. It has no size cap, eviction, or persistence, and no lock guards it. Memory grows without bound, which is a DoS vector when combined with F2. Events are lost on restart, and the store is not shared across worker processes. Appends are safe under the GIL, but iterating while another thread appends is racy for future changes.

produced_findings.claim: Dropping `email` from cached session hashes breaks readers that still expect it The `HEAD` version of the docstring says "session TTL is 24h, so entries written by a previous deploy are routinely still live and read back by a newer one". The delta removes that warning and the `email` field together. `HEAD`'s `read_profile` does `entry["email"]` unconditionally. The new `remember` writes hashes with no `email` key, under the same `session_id` key and with the same 24h TTL. During a rolling deploy, canary or rollback, instances still running the previous code read entries written by the new code and raise `KeyError: 'email'`. This affects every session created or refreshed after the new code starts writing, for up to 24h, and it also hits any other consumer of these hashes. The change also removes the documentation of this constraint, which makes the failure more likely to recur.

produced_findings.claim: Migration drops the index the order-history query depends on The migration calls `RemoveIndex(model_name="order", name="orders_customer_id_idx")`. The unchanged `app/orders/lookup.py:5-11` says `get_orders_for_customer` reads via `orders_customer_id_idx` and runs on every order-history page view. It queries `WHERE customer_id = %s`, and the docstring says one customer can have tens of thousands of orders. The delta adds no replacement index and no change to the query. It also gives no sign that the index is redundant, for example a composite index that covers `customer_id`. Once the migration is applied, the hot-path lookup falls back to a sequential scan of `orders_order`, because no index serves `customer_id`. Every order-history view then scans the whole table. Latency and database load grow with table size, which can degrade or take down the page under production traffic.

Migration file is truncated and fails to parse The file ends right after `name="orders_customer_id_idx",`, at line 13. The `RemoveIndex(` call, the `operations = [` list and the `Migration` class are never closed. The file is 13 lines long and has no closing `),`, `]`, or `)`. I read the file but did not run a parser, because the compile check was not approved. Python raises a `SyntaxError` when the module is imported. Django's migration loader imports every file in the migrations package, so `migrate`, `makemigrations`, `showmigrations` and `manage.py check` can all fail, not only this migration. If this file is committed or deployed as-is, it blocks deploys that run migrations.
